newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN OLOS SEEN SWITCHING FOCUS TO BUDGET, SUPPLY.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN OLOS SEEN SWITCHING FOCUS TO BUDGET, SUPPLY.

text.p: The Belgian linear bond (OLO) market is seen switching focus to upcoming supply and the country's budget after rising on Friday in relief at an in-line U.S. jobs report.

OLOs were pulled higher as Bunds experienced a squeeze after U.S. August non-farm payrolls were reported to have risen 250,000, only slightly higher than a consensus forecast of up 244,000. Unemployment to 5.1 from 5.4 percent.
"The only surprise was perhaps that unemployment fell so much...but I don't think there will be a rate rise now before the (U.S. November 5) election," one trader said.
The U.S. Federal Reserve holds its next policy meeting on September 24, but then does not meet again until November 13.
The yield on OLOs fell to 6.56 percent at one point following the news from 6.62 late on Thursday before settling around 6.59 percent.
But the yield premium over Bunds held around 25 basis points and dealers did not expect Belgium to outperform ahead of new supply at an exchange auction next Tuesday.
"More supply could lead to some underperformance especially if the market continues to go up...the short end can't get much more expensive than it is," a trader at CERA bank said.

At the auction the Treasury is offering OLO lines 13 (7.00 pct April 1999), 25 (5.00 pct March 2001), 24 (7.00 pct May 2006) and 16 (7.50 pct July 2008) in exchange for OLO lines 17 (6.25 pct November 1996) and 22 (7.50 pct January 1997)
Dealers said the budget would also begin to take centre stage as government talks hotted up ahead of an October 1 deadline for its details to be presented to parliament.
Belgian newspaper Le Soir reported on Friday the government was looking for 100 billion francs of savings and additional revenue, with a third coming in new taxes.

OLO dealers and analysts said the number was in line with forecasts with what the market expects the government needs to cut its deficit to three per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), qualifying for European monetary union.
"Most people believe the budget won't be that much of a problem...but there may be some disappointment about the lack of spending cuts," one said.
